---
title: "Price & Performance"
subtitle: "How horsepower, body style, and manufacturer positioning relate to MSRP"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
library(scales)

msrp_df <- read_csv("data/processed/msrp_merged.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
recent_df <- read_csv("data/processed/recent_vehicles_2022_2027.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

n_total_msrp <- nrow(msrp_df)
n_mainstream <- sum(msrp_df$msrp <= 250000)
n_exotic_outliers <- sum(msrp_df$msrp > 250000)
n_recent_hp <- sum(!is.na(recent_df$horsepower_combined))
```

## Overview & Available Performance Variables

To test whether higher vehicle prices buy proportionally more engine performance—or whether buyers primarily pay for body style and brand prestige—we examine **`r comma(n_total_msrp)`** deduplicated new-vehicle observations from [`msrp_merged.csv`](data/processed/msrp_merged.csv) alongside **`r comma(nrow(recent_df))`** recent **2022–2027** trims from [`recent_vehicles_2022_2027.csv`](data/processed/recent_vehicles_2022_2027.csv).

- **Available variables used here:** `horsepower` (engine HP), `msrp` (sticker price in USD), `make` (manufacturer), `model`, `year`, and `body_group` (8 consolidated vehicle body styles).
- **Why torque is omitted:** Inspection of all cleaned datasets confirmed that `torque` is **100% missing** (`0` non-NA values out of `7,397` rows) in Trimslate's public CSV export and is not recorded in either the MSRP dataset or EPA certification tables. Rather than imputing or fabricating values, we focus strictly on verified **horsepower** and **MSRP** records.

---

## 1. Horsepower vs. MSRP Grouped by Vehicle Body Style

To compare the linear dollar-per-horsepower relationship across body styles without million-dollar hypercars compressing the vertical axis, the faceted chart below displays **`r comma(n_mainstream)`** vehicles priced at or below **`$250,000`** (`98.4%` of our `9,762` MSRP observations, excluding **`r n_exotic_outliers`** ultra-exotic outliers up to `$2,065,902`).

::: {.plot-container}
```{r}
#| label: fig-hp-msrp-faceted
#| fig-height: 6.5

# Filter extreme >$250k supercar outliers so linear slopes within each body style are legible
faceted_df <- msrp_df |>
  filter(msrp <= 250000) |>
  mutate(
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", year, " ", make, " ", model, "</b><br>",
      "Body Style: ", body_style, "<br>",
      "Horsepower: ", comma(horsepower), " hp<br>",
      "MSRP: ", dollar(msrp)
    )
  )

p_body_scatter <- ggplot(
  faceted_df,
  aes(x = horsepower, y = msrp, color = body_group)
) +
  geom_point(aes(text = hover_text), alpha = 0.4, size = 1.3) +
  # Linear trend line per body style (inherit.aes = FALSE avoids hover text warnings)
  geom_smooth(
    aes(x = horsepower, y = msrp),
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "#1b2838",
    linewidth = 0.7,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ body_group, ncol = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = " hp")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k")) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "Horsepower vs. MSRP Within Each Body Style (N = ",
      comma(n_mainstream), " Vehicles <= $250k)"
    ),
    x = "Engine Horsepower (hp)",
    y = "MSRP ($ Thousands)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

ggplotly(p_body_scatter, tooltip = "text")
```
:::

**Patterns & Findings:**
Every body style exhibits a positive relationship between horsepower and MSRP, but the **price slope varies dramatically by segment**. **Coupes** and **Convertibles** climb steepest past `300 hp`—frequently crossing `$100,000–$250,000`—whereas **Pickups** and **Vans / Minivans** cluster tightly between `$20,000` and `$55,000` even when equipped with `300–400 hp` V6 and V8 towing engines. **Hatchbacks** occupy the most compact, budget-focused corner (`100–250 hp`, mostly under `$30,000`).

---

## 2. Horsepower per Dollar Across Manufacturers

Which brands deliver the most raw engine output for your money, and which charge a luxury premium? Below, we calculate **horsepower per $1,000 of MSRP** (alongside exact **HP per $1** in the hover tooltip) across all **38 manufacturers** with at least 30 vehicles in our dataset (**`N = 9,681`** vehicles; `81` vehicles from `9` tiny boutique brands with `<30` models are excluded so small samples do not skew brand averages).

::: {.plot-container}
```{r}
#| label: fig-hp-per-dollar-mfr
#| fig-height: 7.5

mfr_summary <- msrp_df |>
  mutate(
    hp_per_1k = horsepower / (msrp / 1000),
    hp_per_dollar = horsepower / msrp
  ) |>
  summarize(
    n_models = n(),
    mean_hp_per_1k = mean(hp_per_1k),
    mean_hp_per_dollar = mean(hp_per_dollar),
    mean_hp = mean(horsepower),
    mean_msrp = mean(msrp),
    .by = make
  ) |>
  filter(n_models >= 30) |>
  mutate(
    make = fct_reorder(make, mean_hp_per_1k),
    tier = case_when(
      mean_msrp >= 100000 ~ "Exotic / Ultra-Luxury (Mean MSRP >= $100k)",
      mean_msrp >= 40000 ~ "Luxury / Near-Luxury ($40k-$99k)",
      TRUE ~ "Mainstream (< $40k)"
    ),
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", make, "</b> (n = ", comma(n_models), " vehicles)<br>",
      "Avg Value: ", round(mean_hp_per_1k, 2), " hp per $1,000 (",
      round(mean_hp_per_dollar, 4), " hp/$)<br>",
      "Avg Horsepower: ", round(mean_hp, 0), " hp<br>",
      "Avg MSRP: ", dollar(round(mean_msrp, 0))
    )
  )

n_mfr_vehicles <- sum(mfr_summary$n_models)

p_mfr <- ggplot(
  mfr_summary,
  aes(x = mean_hp_per_1k, y = make, fill = tier, text = hover_text)
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = " hp/$1k")) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Mainstream (< $40k)" = "#2b8cbe",
      "Luxury / Near-Luxury ($40k-$99k)" = "#7bccc4",
      "Exotic / Ultra-Luxury (Mean MSRP >= $100k)" = "#084081"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "Average Horsepower per $1,000 of MSRP Across 38 Manufacturers (N = ",
      comma(n_mfr_vehicles), " Vehicles)"
    ),
    x = "Average Horsepower per $1,000 of MSRP",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Market Segment"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

ggplotly(p_mfr, tooltip = "text") |>
  layout(
    legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.1),
    margin = list(b = 80)
  )
```
:::

**Patterns & Findings:**
Mainstream brands dominate raw horsepower-per-dollar value: **Dodge** leads all manufacturers at **`9.16 hp` per `$1,000`** (`0.0092 hp/$`, averaging `280 hp` at `$31,182`), followed by **Suzuki (`8.47`)**, **Pontiac (`8.45`)**, **Kia (`8.37`)**, **Chevrolet (`8.12`)**, and **Hyundai (`8.11`)**. Conversely, luxury and exotic badges sit at the bottom—**BMW (`5.44`)**, **Mercedes-Benz (`5.08`)**, **Porsche (`4.01`)**, **Ferrari (`2.23`)**, and **Rolls-Royce (`1.48 hp` per `$1,000`)**—demonstrating diminishing horsepower returns per dollar as buyers pay for craftsmanship, chassis engineering, and brand exclusivity.

---

## 3. Average MSRP Across Vehicle Body Styles

Finally, we compare **average MSRP** across all eight consolidated body styles using the full **`N = `r comma(n_total_msrp)``** dataset (including exotic models, while reporting **median MSRP** and the `<= $250k` trimmed average in each bar's tooltip to show the effect of high-end outliers).

::: {.plot-container}
```{r}
#| label: fig-avg-msrp-body
#| fig-height: 5

body_summary <- msrp_df |>
  summarize(
    n_vehicles = n(),
    mean_msrp = mean(msrp),
    median_msrp = median(msrp),
    trimmed_mean_msrp = mean(msrp[msrp <= 250000]),
    mean_hp = mean(horsepower),
    .by = body_group
  ) |>
  mutate(
    body_group = fct_reorder(body_group, mean_msrp),
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", body_group, "</b> (n = ", comma(n_vehicles), " vehicles)<br>",
      "Average MSRP (all): ", dollar(round(mean_msrp, 0)), "<br>",
      "Median MSRP: ", dollar(round(median_msrp, 0)), "<br>",
      "Average MSRP (<= $250k): ", dollar(round(trimmed_mean_msrp, 0)), "<br>",
      "Average Horsepower: ", round(mean_hp, 0), " hp"
    )
  )

p_body_msrp <- ggplot(
  body_summary,
  aes(x = mean_msrp, y = body_group, text = hover_text)
) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2c3e50", width = 0.68) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "Average MSRP by Vehicle Body Style (N = ",
      comma(n_total_msrp), " Vehicles)"
    ),
    x = "Average MSRP (USD)",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplotly(p_body_msrp, tooltip = "text")
```
:::

**Patterns & Findings:**
**Convertibles (`$96,084` mean; `$49,850` median)** and **Coupes (`$92,495` mean; `$46,150` median)** carry more than double the average MSRP of any other body style—partly because almost all six- and seven-figure supercars take two-door coupe or roadster form (even excluding `>$250k` exotics, Convertibles average `$72,145` and Coupes `$68,079`). Mainstream utility and family styles sit much closer to their medians: **Sedans (`$45,424` mean / `$32,970` median)**, **SUVs (`$41,313` mean / `$35,800` median)**, **Pickups (`$32,724`)**, **Vans / Minivans (`$30,603`)**, **Wagons (`$30,120`)**, and entry-level **Hatchbacks (`$23,364`)**.

---

## Limitations: Comparing 2001–2017 MSRP Data With 2022–2027 Vehicles

Because our price analysis relies on [`msrp_merged.csv`](data/processed/msrp_merged.csv) (**2001–2017**) while our recent specification tabs use [`recent_vehicles_2022_2027.csv`](data/processed/recent_vehicles_2022_2027.csv) (**2022–2027**), three concrete limitations apply:

1. **Post-2017 price inflation is not captured in nominal MSRPs:** U.S. new-vehicle transaction and sticker prices rose substantially after 2020, so a `$33,050` median MSRP in our 2001–2017 data reflects earlier nominal dollars rather than 2022–2027 showroom stickers.
2. **Higher baseline horsepower in 2022–2027:** Across the **`r comma(n_recent_hp)`** recent 2022–2027 trims with certified engine output, horsepower averages **`r round(mean(recent_df$horsepower_combined, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` hp** (median **`r round(median(recent_df$horsepower_combined, na.rm = TRUE), 0)` hp**), up from **`r round(mean(msrp_df$horsepower), 1)` hp** (median **`r round(median(msrp_df$horsepower), 0)` hp**) in our 2001–2017 MSRP dataset due to widespread turbocharging and larger SUV/truck lineups.
3. **Electrified powertrain gaps:** Modern battery-electric vehicles (EVs) and full hybrids—which play a major role in 2022–2027 pricing and acceleration—had minimal market share prior to 2017 and frequently lack combined system horsepower in EPA engine-certification tables. For those vehicles, we avoid merging incompatible years and instead examine recent powertrains directly on the **[Fuel Economy](fuel.qmd)** and **[Car Explorer](explorer.qmd)** pages.
